newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Foreign interests in Hong Kong to be "accommodated".
newsitem.headline: Foreign interests in Hong Kong to be "accommodated".

text.p: Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen said on Wednesday Hong Kong's current laws would be "basically maintained" and foreign economic interests accommodated after the British colony reverted to Chinese rule next July 1.
"Hong Kong will retain its status as an international trade, financial and shipping center, free port and separate customs territory," he told the General Assembly.
"Its long-term stability and prosperity will be guaranteed. Foreign economic interests in Hong Kong will be accommodated," he added, without elaborating.
Qian said the resumption of Chinese sovereignty would be a "milestone in the great cause of our national reunification."

"As a special administrative region of the People's Republic of China and in conformity with the Basic Law of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, Hong Kong will be administered by the Hong Kong people," he said.
"It will enjoy a high degree of autonomy. The existing social and economic system and way of life will remain unchanged and the laws currently in force in Hong Kong will be basically maintained."
Referring to the transfer of sovereignty, he said: "We have thereby set a good example of countries peacefully resolving issues left over by history...

"We are fully capable of ensuring a smooth transfer of government and transition in Hong Kong. After Hong Kong's return to the embrace of the motherland, we will put into effect the policy of 'one country, two systems.'"
On the issue of Taiwan, which China regards as a renegade province, Qian said: "There is but one China in the world, and Taiwan is an inalienable part of the sacred territory of China.
"Peaceful reunification and one country, two systems -- this is our unswerving guideline for settlement of the Taiwan question," he said.

Alluding to efforts to obtain U.N. membership for Taiwan -- defeated in the General Assembly's steering committee last week for the fourth successive year -- he said the question of China's representation in the United Nations was settled by a 1971 resolution.
That resolution expelled the Chinese Nationalist government on Taiwan, which until then had held China's U.N. seat, and gave the seat to the Communist government in Beijing.
The question of Taiwan "involves a cardinal principle of China's sovereignty, territorial integrity and reunification," Qian said.

"It is purely China's internal affair which brooks no outside interference. The Chinese government and people are determined to carry through the struggle against all attempts to split their territory or create an independent Taiwan. No force on earth can hold back China's cause of reunification," he said.
